html:
The longer I live in white-majority societies, the more I find that racism is deeply rooted, you could even say innate. Once you realize that, you feel you shouldn’t really blame the individuals who discriminate against you: it’s a fixed way of thinking, created by the whole society and impossible to avoid. Of course, that doesn’t stop you from saying “f*** you” when it happens, and flipping them the bird while you’re at it.

Picture this: on a pitch-dark road, a big, burly Black man comes toward you, and so does an equally big, burly white man. What goes through your mind?

I think nine people out of ten would feel the white man is safer.


I haven’t lived in the Netherlands as long as in Germany, but I’ve experienced much more discrimination here. A bunch of kids surrounded me outside a supermarket pulling slant-eye faces. Someone took my seat at the cinema, and when I asked for it back I got a “f*** you.” Random guys have come up to me on the street and been abusive. Someone poured water down from an upstairs window as I walked past a house (maybe I’m being oversensitive and it wasn’t aimed at me). What do you do when this happens? Shout “f*** you” right back and flip them the bird, of course. After enough times, you stop being surprised.

The odd thing is that although I hardly ever met open racism in Germany, I still prefer the Netherlands.

Isn’t that just masochistic?

Well, you could say so. There’s less overt racism in Germany, but that doesn’t mean Germans are fairer than the Dutch. It just means the discrimination is more implicit and better hidden. That has to do with the German character, which for historical reasons keeps many things unsaid. If a German doesn’t like you, he won’t tell you; he’ll simply ignore you. The Dutch are the opposite: they pride themselves on being open and direct. If they don’t like you or your country, they’ll say so to your face.

To use an imperfect analogy: would you rather deal with someone who stabs you in the back, or someone who argues with you to your face?

I prefer people who say what they mean. At least it’s honest. German arrogance and that deep-seated pride are clearly there; the Dutch have them too, but not as strongly.

Today I was chatting with a colleague. My Dutch colleague said he’s been coaching his son’s soccer team lately, and that the Turkish kids are hard to coach: “f***ing Turkish.” I asked why. Is it because in the evenings they’re too dark to see?

Race is deeply rooted in his mind. He hates French arrogance, American fakeness, German rigidity, East Europeans’ ugly English accents, Spaniards’ overlong coffee breaks, South Americans’ loose morals, and of course he never misses a chance to wheel out the usual old stereotypes about the Chinese. When I’m in a good mood, I joke along; when I’m not, I snap back at him. Life goes on.

What can you do about him? However hard you argue, with all the facts and reasoning in the world, trying to make him (or them) drop stereotypes formed in childhood is completely unrealistic.

If you can make peace with it and accept it, stay. If you can’t, or you don’t want to put up with it? Go home. The world is a big place, and being happy is what matters most.
